title: Stack and queue explained: LIFO vs FIFO, Python code and complexity — cv.cm
description: Stacks (LIFO) and queues (FIFO) explained with Python code: list as a stack, collections.deque as a queue, bracket matching, BFS and complexity.
h1: Stack and queue explained: LIFO vs FIFO with Python examples
answer: A stack is a collection where the last item added is the first one removed (LIFO, last in first out), like a pile of plates. A queue is a collection where the first item added is the first one removed (FIFO, first in first out), like a line at a checkout. Both support adding and removing in O(1) time. In Python, use a `list` as a stack and `collections.deque` as a queue.

sections.h: What problem stacks and queues solve
body: Many programs need to remember items and process them later in a fixed order. A stack gives you the most recent item first, which matches nested work: function calls, undo history, matching brackets, and depth-first search. A queue gives you the oldest item first, which matches fair waiting: print jobs, task schedulers, message queues and breadth-first search.
Both are abstract data types: they are defined by their operations, not by how they are stored. You can build either one on top of an array or a linked list.

sections.h: Worked example: push and pop step by step
body: Push 1, 2 and 3 into both structures, then remove two items.

A Python `list` is already a good stack: `append` and `pop()` work on the end of the list in O(1) amortized time. For a queue, do not use `list.pop(0)`, because it shifts every remaining element and costs O(n). Use `collections.deque`, which is O(1) at both ends.

body.code:
from collections import deque
stack = []
stack.append(1)
stack.append(2)
stack.append(3)
print(stack.pop(), stack[-1])   # 3 2
queue = deque()
queue.append("a")
queue.append("b")
queue.append("c")
print(queue.popleft(), queue[0])  # a b
print(len(stack), len(queue))     # 2 2

To check that every bracket is closed in the right order, push each opening bracket. When you see a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its matching opener.
The same idea evaluates expressions in reverse Polish notation, converts recursion into a loop, and drives depth-first search: replace the call stack with your own list.
Breadth-first search visits a graph level by level. A queue makes that happen: nodes discovered first are processed first.
Amortized means that an occasional `append` resizes the underlying array and costs O(n), but averaged over many operations each one is O(1).

ul: Deque (double-ended queue): add and remove at both ends. `collections.deque` is one, and it can act as both a stack and a queue.
Priority queue: removes the smallest (or largest) item first, not the oldest. Use `heapq`; see the binary heap page.
Circular buffer: a fixed-size queue stored in an array with wrapping indexes. `deque(maxlen=n)` drops the oldest item when full.
Thread-safe queues: `queue.Queue` for threads and `asyncio.Queue` for coroutines block while waiting for items.
A queue built from two stacks: push to an in-stack, and when the out-stack is empty move everything across. Each item moves once, so operations are O(1) amortized.

body.note: Calling `pop()` on an empty `list` or `popleft()` on an empty `deque` raises `IndexError`. Check `if stack:` before popping, or catch the exception.

faq.q: What is the difference between a stack and a queue?
faq.a: A stack removes the most recently added item first (LIFO). A queue removes the oldest item first (FIFO). Both add and remove in O(1) time.

faq.q: Should I use a list or deque for a queue in Python?
faq.a: Use `collections.deque`. Removing from the front of a `list` with `pop(0)` is O(n) because all other elements shift; `deque.popleft()` is O(1).

faq.q: Where is a stack used in real programs?
faq.a: The call stack that stores function calls, undo and redo history, browser back buttons, expression parsing, bracket matching and depth-first search.
It happens when the call stack runs out of space, usually because of very deep or infinite recursion. In Python it shows up as `RecursionError` when the recursion limit is exceeded.

faq.q: Is queue.Queue the same as collections.deque?
faq.a: No. `queue.Queue` is a thread-safe queue with locking and blocking `get` and `put`, meant for passing work between threads. `collections.deque` is a faster general-purpose container without blocking.
